alignment.note: ἔρχονται / ܘܐܬܘ / veniunt — the Syriac prefixes the conjunction to the verb (ܘܐܬܘ), so token 0 carries both the 'and' and 'they came' senses.

Greek uses preposition εἰς + accusative Ἱεροσόλυμα (with the transliteration token bound to it); Syriac and Latin both express directional motion synthetically — Syriac with the prefixed lamadh (ܠܐܘܪܫܠܡ) and Latin with the bare accusative of place (Jerosolymam) without a preposition.

The clausal connector καί introducing the temporal circumstance is rendered in Syriac by the compound ܘܟܕ ('and when') and in Latin split across Et + cum, the latter governing the subjunctive of attendant circumstance.

Greek employs a genitive absolute (περιπατοῦντος αὐτοῦ) with locative ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ; Latin renders this with a cum-clause and imperfect subjunctive (cum ambularet in templo), while Syriac uses the periphrastic past with the auxiliary ܗܘܐ (ܡܗܠܟ ܗܘܐ ܒܗܝܟܠܐ) — three different syntactic strategies for the same backgrounded action.
ἔρχονται / ܐܬܘ / accedunt — the Greek repeats ἔρχομαι resumptively after the absolute; Latin sharpens it to accedunt ('approach').
πρὸς αὐτόν / ܠܘܬܗ / ad eum — Syriac compresses preposition and pronominal object into a single inflected form.
οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς / ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ / summi sacerdotes — all three render the title with a construct/superlative phrase ('chiefs of the priests').
οἱ γραμματεῖς / ܘܣܦܪܐ / scribæ — Syriac binds the conjunction to the noun (ܘܣܦܪܐ), here grouped with the connector above; lexically ܣܦܪܐ 'scribes' aligns with γραμματεῖς.
οἱ πρεσβύτεροι / ܘܩܫܝܫܐ / seniores — Syriac again carries the conjunction on the noun; the root q-sh-sh denotes the elders' seniority, cognate with Arabic قِسِّيس.
The Vulgate closes the verse with a colon anticipating the direct discourse of the following verse; neither the Greek nor the Syriac transmits a corresponding punctuation token here.
